finding.claim: Authorization check on DELETE /files/<fid> is a no-op: require_allowed (alias of acl.is_allowed, which returns a bool and never aborts) is called without using its return value, so any caller, including one with no grant, can delete any file in STORE.
finding.source: HTTP header X-Session-User-Verified read into g.user at views.py:12 (attacker-controlled; nothing in this repo verifies or sets it). Also the fid path parameter at views.py:16.
finding.sink: views.py:19 del STORE[fid] — destructive deletion of a stored file.

trace.note: g.user taken straight from request header; no verification in this repo
require_allowed(g.user, f, 'delete') imported as is_allowed (views.py:4); return value discarded, so no abort/raise happens even when denied
is_allowed returns a boolean; it does not call abort

finding.guards_checked: before_request sets g.user only (no auth). is_allowed returns False for unlisted users, but the result is ignored at views.py:18. Contrast rename_file at views.py:26, which uses ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10, calls abort(403)) and is correct. Confirmed by comparing the two handlers line by line: the alias rename hides the bug because the name looks like an enforcing call.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. views.py:4 aliases acl.is_allowed (acl.py:4-5, returns a bool, never aborts) as require_allowed, and views.py:18 calls it as a bare statement with its result discarded. views.py:19 then runs del STORE[fid] unconditionally. The only other control, views.py:10-12 before_request, copies the header into g.user with no verification. The helper that does enforce, ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10, aborts with 403), is used only by rename_file at views.py:26.
verdict.reason: The delete handler at views.py:18 discards the bool from is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) instead of calling ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10), so views.py:19 deletes the file for any g.user, including one with no grant. An anonymous or low-privilege caller can reach this, since the identity in views.py:12 is not verified in this repo; an upstream authenticating proxy, if one exists, is not visible here, and the missing enforcement is a bug either way.

finding.claim: Caller identity is taken from a client-supplied header named 'Verified' with no code in the repo that verifies it, so any client can impersonate any user listed in the grants map (acl.py:5) by sending that user's name in the header.
finding.source: HTTP request header X-Session-User-Verified (views.py:12), fully attacker-controlled unless an upstream proxy strips and sets it. The repo contains no proxy config or signature check.
finding.sink: Authorization decision in acl.py:5 (grants lookup) used by views.py:26 (rename, write) and views.py:18 (delete, which is already bypassed by F1).

trace.note: grants.get(user) keyed only on the header value

finding.guards_checked: No signature, session cookie, or token validation anywhere in the repo. The header name suggests an upstream verifier that is not part of this repository, so this is a precondition to confirm with the deployment, not a confirmed exploit. If the proxy does not strip client-supplied values, this is exploitable.

verdict.guard_found: None in the repo. views.py:12 reads the header with no signature, cookie, or token check, and acl.py:5 keys grants solely on that value. ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) does abort(403) when the check fails, and views.py:26 does not discard that result, so it is a real gate, but it only compares the attacker-supplied name. The only possible upstream control, a proxy that strips and sets X-Session-User-Verified, is not in this repo.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code (views.py:12 → views.py:26 → acl.py:5), and nothing in the repo validates the header, but whether a client can reach this depends on whether an upstream proxy at deployment strips and sets X-Session-User-Verified, which this repo cannot show. Minor correction: the header is X-Session-User-Verified, not 'Verified' as the claim says.

finding.claim: Unknown fid raises KeyError instead of returning 404 on both DELETE and rename handlers, causing unhandled 500 responses. Low severity; it is a robustness issue, not a security boundary.
finding.sink: STORE[fid] lookup at views.py:17 and views.py:25.

trace.note: f = STORE[fid] with no membership check

finding.guards_checked: No try/except or STORE.get. Included for completeness only; it does not affect the authorization outcome.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only pre-handler hook is load_user at views.py:10-12, which reads a header and does not check membership or abort. The lookups at views.py:17 and views.py:25 are bare STORE[fid] with no try/except or STORE.get, so an unknown fid raises KeyError before require_allowed (line 18) or ensure_allowed (line 26) runs.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: views.py:17 and views.py:25 both do a bare STORE[fid] lookup with no prior check, so any requester (including anonymous, since load_user at views.py:11-12 does not block) who sends DELETE /files/<unknown> or POST /files/<unknown>/rename triggers an unhandled KeyError that Flask turns into a 500. This is a real but low-severity robustness issue, not an authorization bypass, so the candidate's own severity assessment holds.
